title: General atomically precise covalent construction

concept.text: The envisioned innovation is a programmable method for building covalently bonded structures by placing atoms or molecular fragments at selected positions and making the intended bonds, repeatedly. A designer would specify atomic connectivity, and an instrument would carry out a sequence of chemical operations to construct it. The target extends across diverse elements and build environments and includes structures that grow out of the starting surface into three dimensions. This remains a proposed capability.

Scanning-probe mechanosynthesis provides a concrete starting point: a probe controls the relative position of a reactive molecular tool and a target site so that a chemical transformation can occur locally. The supplied review describes Cowie and colleagues’ demonstration of carbon-fragment placement and successive carbon–carbon bond formation on hydrogenated silicon. General construction would extend those operations into a reusable repertoire for building larger, chemically varied structures, including continued assembly above the original surface.

significance.text: If achieved with sufficient chemical breadth and reliability, this would establish a fabrication principle based on designer-selected atomic placement and covalent connectivity. It could make particular structures accessible when conventional reaction pathways do not readily select them. The reported positional control and assigned, previously unreported surface-bound C4 structure provide a limited experimental basis for that possibility within one surface chemistry.

Conditional synthesis: direct benefits could include deliberately positioned defects, selected molecular junctions and structures whose useful behavior depends on precise local bonding. Functional molecular devices would additionally require control of electronic or mechanical properties, stability, contacts, integration and operation. Successful construction alone would not establish those functions.

The analogy to a general-purpose fabrication system has important limits. Chemistry already produces many precisely defined molecules, and lithography is more varied than simply carving statistical materials. The distinctive ambition here is repeatable positional control over an expanding range of covalent construction operations. Even several successful products would not establish the ability to build arbitrary stable atomic arrangements: stability does not guarantee an accessible assembly pathway, suitable reagents or probe access.

Conditional scaling assessment: useful macroscopic production would require further advances in throughput and parallelism, as well as reliable reagent supply, error management and handling of completed products. The supplied evidence contains no scaling analysis that would justify a production rate, cost estimate or timetable for bulk manufacturing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is a reusable sequence of position-controlled covalent reactions that continues working as a structure grows, across multiple elements and build environments. The reviewed paper identifies reliable placement of reactive fragments and iterative chemical operations as prerequisites for controlled out-of-plane assembly. Its introduction describes reliable synthesis of extended structures through out-of-plane bonding as a remaining challenge at the time of the May 2026 submission.

Engineering synthesis: broader construction requires reactions that make the intended bond while avoiding competing reactions, unwanted attachment to the tool, damage to the existing product and loss of reactive fragments. A useful toolkit must also support reagent delivery, tool regeneration or replacement, and product termination. Operations demonstrated for one carbon-bearing molecular-tool family on hydrogenated silicon do not by themselves establish compatible operations for other transferred elements or surfaces.

Engineering synthesis: three-dimensional growth adds geometric and mechanical barriers. The probe must reach new reaction sites without colliding with previously assembled material; the growing structure must remain sufficiently stable and constrained for accurate positioning; and changing local environments must not invalidate the reaction sequence. Larger products also require errors to be detected and corrected or otherwise contained before repeated operations accumulate unacceptable defects.

Engineering synthesis: programmability requires translating a desired structure into an executable reaction sequence with sufficiently predictable outcomes, without bespoke human redesign for every product. Verification must distinguish intended connectivity from a visually similar placement pattern. These requirements connect chemical control, instrumentation, planning and measurement; none is established generally by a small set of surface-bound products.

current_state.text: Cowie et al.’s arXiv preprint, arXiv:2605.27250, was submitted on 26 May 2026. According to the supplied review of the main-paper text, the authors report donation of C2 units from surface-deposited molecular tools to hydrogen-passivated Si(100), using inverted-mode scanning tunneling microscopy at 4 K. This is a reported experimental advance in controlled carbon construction under cryogenic conditions, within one molecular-tool family and one build-surface chemistry.

The reported X-shaped pattern contains nine C2 units, comprising 18 deliberately patterned carbon atoms. That count describes separate units arranged on the surface; it does not establish a single connected 18-carbon covalent product and does not include substrate atoms. The paper also reports successive C2 donation and carbon–carbon bond formation yielding assigned C4 structures. Those chain-extension results are more informative about iterative chemistry than the placement pattern alone, while remaining far short of extended three-dimensional construction.

The structural assignments described in the supplied review rely on STM observations and calculations. The review had the full extracted main-paper text, including figure captions and discussion, but lacked figure images and supplementary materials. This supports an account of what the authors report; it does not provide independent structural validation or a complete assessment of the underlying experimental evidence. Those access limits do not show that the reported results are false.

The earlier claim that the HTML was dated 24 August 2026 is unverified. The retained HTML described in the review is an abstract and metadata page that establishes the May submission date but contains no August date. The supplied bounded search record is empty, so subsequent developments and the field-wide absence of a general constructor as of 1 November 2026 remain unestablished. The evidence supports a dated, narrow demonstration and the paper’s stated technical challenge.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: one instrument builds at least three chemically distinct, pre-specified covalent structures, each containing approximately 10^2 to 10^3 deliberately assembled product atoms, without human redesign of the chemistry for each product. The products should include bonding and continued growth out of the starting plane, with site-resolved verification of intended connectivity. Cryogenic ultrahigh-vacuum operation could be allowed initially. The product count, atom range and operating allowance are proposed thresholds, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: One instrument builds three distinct ~100–1,000-atom structures without chemistry redesign

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth requirement: the demonstrations should span more than one transferred element and more than one substrate or build environment. Otherwise, three different products could satisfy the original wording while relying on essentially the same narrow chemistry. A finite test would establish demonstrated breadth over its tested operations and environments; it would not prove literal universality or access to every stable atomic arrangement.
completion_criteria.label: Construction spans multiple transferred elements and substrates or build environments

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification and reproducibility requirements: disclose the construction sequences, molecular tools, operating conditions, successful and failed attempts, and evidence used to assign bonds. Repeat construction of the same targets across independent runs, and seek replication by an independent group. Report operation-level reliability, whole-product yield, construction time and any human intervention. Verification should resolve connectivity rather than relying only on a pattern’s overall shape.
completion_criteria.label: Connectivity-verified construction repeats across runs with procedures and performance disclosed

completion_criteria.text: The paper’s distinction between reliable fragment placement and iterative chemical operations provides the scientific basis for requiring both in a convincing demonstration. A single C2 transfer, or a pattern of separately placed C2 units, does not meet the proposed construction milestone. Practical boundaries should also be explicit: success at 4 K would establish capability under those conditions, while ambient operation, product removal, device function and useful manufacturing throughput would remain separate achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Construction combines fragment placement and iterative chemistry with explicit boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MAS-04, “A reliable map from a property specification to a makeable material,” addresses choosing a material and a feasible route from desired properties. MAS-03 addresses executing precise covalent construction. A successful MAS-03 platform could expand the structures available to an MAS-04 design system, but would not itself solve prediction of properties or selection of the right material.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-07, “Programmable growth of load-bearing solids,” overlaps in controlled growth. MAS-03 emphasizes atomic placement and covalent connectivity across chemistries, whereas MAS-07 requires growth that produces useful structural material. Atomic construction could contribute local control, but load-bearing scale, growth rate and mechanical performance remain additional requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-02, “Bulk structural solids that are both near their ideal strength and damage-tolerant,” MAS-05, “Structural solids that remain engineering materials after fusion-level atomic displacement,” and MAS-09, “Structural metals that fully recover from macroscopic fracture in service,” concern mechanical performance, irradiation survival and in-service recovery. Precise construction might help investigate selected defects or local structures relevant to these goals. It would not establish bulk toughness, radiation tolerance or autonomous fracture repair.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-01, “Ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductivity in a manufacturable solid,” and MAS-10, “Topologically protected quantum matter outside the dilution refrigerator,” concern emergent electronic states under demanding operating conditions. Atomic construction could potentially help make selected structures or interfaces for investigation. Their superconducting or topological behavior, operating temperature and manufacturability would require separate evidence; covalent placement alone establishes none of them.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-06, “Reversible solids that store energy at chemical-fuel specific energy,” and MAS-08, “An ambient catalytic solid that fixes nitrogen at industrial intensity,” could benefit from precise control of bonding or active-site environments. Their defining requirements concern reversible energy storage and catalytic performance, respectively. Building a selected structure would leave energy density, reversibility, reaction rate, stability and industrial operation to be demonstrated independently.

unresolved_issues: Whether subsequent work established broader construction capability by 1 November 2026 cannot be determined from the empty supplied freshness record.
The asserted 24 August 2026 HTML date remains unverified; its origin is not established.
Independent assessment of the reported structural assignments remains limited by the absence of figure images and supplementary materials from the supplied review.
Independent replication, complete operation-level reliability, whole-product yields and scaling performance are not established by the supplied material.

The proposed milestone still requires choices about which elements, environments and verification methods would constitute a sufficiently demanding breadth test; its numerical thresholds are proposals.

brief.title: Building structures with atoms placed to order
possible: A designer could specify which atoms connect, then have an instrument build that structure through repeated chemical steps. Construction could grow above its starting surface and work with varied elements and surroundings.
This could make structures that ordinary chemical reactions do not readily produce, including molecular connections whose behavior depends on exactly where atoms sit and how they bond.
why: For researchers making molecular devices, control over individual bonds would offer a way to build deliberately chosen structures. They could place connections and defects exactly where a design needs them.

sources.who: Megan Cowie and colleagues, CBN Nano Technologies
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reported placing carbon fragments at chosen sites on silicon and joining them through successive chemical bonds under extreme cold.
sources.quote:
Here, we demonstrate simultaneous spatial and chemical control over the mechanosynthetic fab-
rication of carbon structures.
sources.cited_for: This supports both controlled fragment placement and repeated bond formation.
sources.not_established: Small surface-bound carbon products do not establish reusable construction across varied elements or extended growth above a surface.

sources.who: Brandon Blue, Mathieu Morin and colleagues, CBN Nano Technologies
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reported adding carbon fragments and removing silicon atoms at selected surface sites with molecular tools.
sources.quote:
we demonstrate positionally-controlled mechanosynthetic addition 
(donation) of carbon and subtraction (abstraction) of silicon atoms on a model build site: 
atomically clean and crystalline Si(100).
sources.cited_for: This supports a broader set of local construction operations, including material removal.
sources.not_established: Adding and removing material on silicon does not establish a general method for building larger, chemically varied structures.

sources.who: Qigang Zhong and colleagues, Justus Liebig University Giessen
sources.showed: The team selectively joined molecular building blocks on a salt film and tracked individual bonds with microscope images.
sources.quote:
Further demonstrations of 
structural build-up include complex bonding motifs, like carbon–iodine–carbon bonds and fused carbon pentagons.
sources.cited_for: This supports selective assembly of connected molecules with direct examination of their bonds.
sources.not_established: The surface-based assembly does not establish continued construction above the surface or a broadly reusable chemical toolkit.

sources.who: Jie Su, Jiali Li and colleagues
sources.showed: The team combined artificial intelligence with probe chemistry to make magnetic carbon molecules with control over individual bonds.
sources.quote: allowing for atomically precise single-molecule manipulation to fabricate single-molecule quantum π-magnets with single-bond precision.
sources.cited_for: This supports using artificial intelligence to guide precise chemical changes in individual molecules.
sources.not_established: Precise changes to selected molecules do not establish general construction from designer-specified atomic connections.

shown: Cowie and colleagues reported extending carbon fragments into structures assigned to contain four carbon atoms. Microscope observations and calculations support those assignments. This is a small demonstration from a single group, reported in a preprint.
Other teams have selectively joined molecular building blocks and used artificial intelligence to guide individual bond changes. These demonstrate useful pieces of the proposed capability.
missing: A reusable set of reactions must keep making the intended bonds as structures grow above the starting surface.
Construction must work across different transferred elements and build environments.
A desired structure must translate into a reliable chemical sequence without bespoke redesign for each product.
Larger builds need dependable material delivery, tool replacement and error management.

milestones.label: One instrument builds three chemically distinct structures
milestones.explanation: Targets of roughly hundreds of deliberately assembled atoms would need verified bonds and growth above the surface, without chemistry redesign between products. This would test reusable construction.

milestones.label: Construction works across elements and build environments
milestones.explanation: Construction would have to transfer different elements and work on different surfaces or in different environments. This would establish breadth beyond a narrow chemistry.

milestones.label: Verified construction repeats with disclosed procedures and performance
milestones.explanation: Repeated runs would need verified bonds, disclosed procedures, failures, reliability, yield, time and human involvement, with independent replication sought. This would establish reproducibility.

milestones.label: Placement and repeated bond formation work together
milestones.explanation: Construction would have to combine fragment placement with repeated chemical reactions and state its operating limits. This would distinguish assembly from a placement pattern and define what success establishes.

uncertain: Which elements, environments and bond measurements would make a sufficiently demanding test of general construction remains open.
Independent replication and the reliability of complete builds remain unestablished.
Whether these operations can reach useful production rates remains unknown.

page.title: Programmable covalent mechanosynthesis
page.definition: Mechanosynthesis directs bond formation by mechanically positioning reactive atoms or molecular fragments. A programmable instrument would use a reusable reaction repertoire to build specified covalent structures, continue growth above the starting surface and work with different transferred elements and build environments.

goal.need: Molecular electronics and semiconductor quantum devices require control of atomic composition, bonding and position. Cowie et al. report nine separately placed C2 units, comprising 18 carbon atoms, and assigned C4 products on hydrogenated silicon at 4 K. Extending this control to programmed construction requires sequences that keep making specified bonds as a product grows. The tool-dependent outcomes below quantify the selectivity of individual operations.

figures.caption: Reported outcomes for vertical approach-and-retract trajectories targeting silicon dimers.
figures.note: The tools perform different reactions. These are interaction-level outcomes, not complete-product yields. The preprint was submitted on 11 June 2026 and is not peer reviewed.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: The goal of this program is to achieve complete control over the placement of atoms and molecules
statements.context: The atom-scale devices programme concerns fabrication, characterization and validation of solid-state devices; its page was updated on 5 October 2026.

statements.quote: chemically bind the feedstock to a growing structure or device at that attachment point;
statements.context: One operation in the integrated-nanosystem target under Topic 7(a), Molecular Machine Advances, in the FY 2018 SBIR/STTR solicitation. The target also includes feedstock transport, positioning and repetition to produce a defect-free product.

statements.quote: One of the grand challenges of nanoscience is precise positioning, atom by atom.

completion.title: A programmable system builds specified covalent structures across chemistries in three dimensions.
completion.criterion: An instrument executes a supplied construction programme using a reusable repertoire of position-controlled reactions to make pre-specified covalent structures, with continued growth above the starting surface. Demonstrations change both the transferred element and the build environment while retaining programmed construction; experimental characterization establishes product connectivity. This operational test sets no atom-count, yield or temperature cutoff and does not establish the ability to build arbitrary stable atomic arrangements.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; operational interpretation of the cited programme and research-roadmap goals.
completion.basis: Searched DOE APM targets, NIST programme goals, Productive Nanosystems and IMM roadmaps, standards searches and Feynman prize specifications; no completion test covering different transferred elements and build environments was located. DOE supplies the repeated feedstock-to-product cycle; the roadmaps supply three-dimensional growth, chemistry extension and blueprint control. Their combination is an Atlas interpretation.

milestones.title: A positioned atom or molecular fragment chemically binds at a specified atomic site.
milestones.criterion: The attachment-stage objective is chemical binding of positioned feedstock to a growing structure at its specified atomic position. Oyabu et al., published on 2 May 2003, mechanically removed selected silicon atoms and deposited single atoms into vacancies on Si(111)-(7×7), without applied bias or voltage pulses. Zhong et al. subsequently demonstrated covalent dimers and trimers on two-layer NaCl/Cu(111) at approximately 5.2 K using voltage-driven probe operations in 2021.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, FY 2018 SBIR/STTR Topics, Topic 7(a), positioning and attachment objectives.

milestones.title: A workpiece undergoes at least two mechanosynthetic reactions near the same reactive site.
milestones.criterion: At least two reactions occur on or near the same reactive site of one workpiece, driven by mechanical forces without an electric field driving those reactions. Cowie et al.'s preprint, submitted on 26 May 2026, reports successive C2 transfers and assigned C4 products on hydrogenated Si(100) at 4 K. This silicon experiment bears on the reaction-sequence benchmark; the preprint is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: IMM contributors to the Technology Roadmap for Productive Nanosystems, proposed mechanosynthesis milestone 5; a published research benchmark, not an established consensus standard.

milestones.title: A repeatable reaction sequence builds a verified diamondoid structure on diamond.
milestones.criterion: A repeatable sequence of diamondoid mechanosynthesis operations on a diamond surface produces a new, experimentally verified diamondoid structure. Diamondoid denotes a framework with diamond-like tetrahedral bonding. The cited carbon-transfer experiments use silicon surfaces and do not establish this diamond-specific result.
milestones.set_by: IMM contributors to the Technology Roadmap for Productive Nanosystems, proposed milestone 6, explicitly written for diamond.
milestones.threshold_quote: a new diamondoid structure on that surface

milestones.title: Mechanical bond formation constructs a three-dimensional diamondoid object.
milestones.criterion: Purely mechanical synthesis constructs a three-dimensional diamondoid object, with roadmap examples including rods, prisms and objects containing holes. The source calls the object significant but supplies no minimum atom count or dimension. An assigned surface-bound C4 product alone does not establish this object-level benchmark.
milestones.set_by: Freitas and Merkle, IMM Nanofactory Roadmap, Task I-10 benchmark F; proposed for diamondoid construction.

milestones.title: A workstation builds atomically precise diamondoid products incorporating elements beyond C, H and Ge.
milestones.criterion: Task I-11 extends positional fabrication to a variety of atomically precise diamondoid structures incorporating elements beyond carbon, hydrogen and germanium. It permits changes to feedstocks, tools, reaction sequences and fabrication surfaces, and permits one-off products without parallelization. Silicon abstraction in Blue et al. removes substrate atoms; it does not establish incorporation of additional elements into these products.
milestones.set_by: Freitas and Merkle, IMM Nanofactory Roadmap, Task I-11; a proposed chemistry-extension target for diamondoid workstations.
milestones.threshold_quote: atoms in addition to carbon, hydrogen and germanium.

milestones.title: Computer control fabricates a covalent nanostructure from a blueprint without intervention for each reaction.
milestones.criterion: Computer-controlled tip trajectories, rotations and positioning execute the mechanosynthetic fabrication process according to a blueprint without human intervention for each reaction. Su et al. reported AI-assisted probe chemistry and synchronous six-bond transformations in individual nanographenes in 2024. That molecular transformation alone does not establish autonomous fabrication of a complete structure from a blueprint.
milestones.set_by: IMM contributors to the Technology Roadmap for Productive Nanosystems, proposed milestone 2, the blueprint-controlled fabrication objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: without direct intervention of a human operator for each reaction.

not_found: No external completion criterion spanning transferred elements and build environments was located in the programme, roadmap, standards and prize searches.
The cited roadmaps do not establish field-wide adoption of their proposed benchmarks.
No experimental report meeting the cited three-dimensional diamondoid or multi-element workstation targets was located.
No independent replication of the CBN carbon-transfer and chain-extension results was located.

results.finding: Site-specific C2 donation on silicon produced IR-C2 in 184 of 197 attempts.
results.detail: The assigned product was formed by approach and retraction at 0 V, after electrically preparing the reactive site and tool.
results.quote:
The build sequence in Fig. 5 demonstrates positional and chemical control over mechanosynthetic C2 donation, with
high yields: 93% for IR-C 2 (184/197, 95% confidence interval 89-96%), 97% for 2IR-C2 (71/73, 95% confidence
interval 91-99%), 92% for IR-C2/C4 (45/49, 95% confidence interval 81-97%), and 84% for 2IR-C 4 (27/32, 95%
confidence interval 68-93%).

results.finding: Successive C2 transfers produced an assigned IR-C4 beside IR-C2 in 45 of 49 attempts.
results.detail: A second C2 donation extended the first surface-bound C2 unit. The transfer reactions used mechanical approach and retraction at 0 V; the C4 structure was assigned from imaging and simulation.
results.quote:
Four successive C 2 transfers generate an eight-carbon pattern with site-specific
placement.

results.finding: Positioned C2 donation occurred in 107 of 197 interactions on Si(100).
results.detail: Interactions targeted the silicon dimer center without applied bias during the reaction. Product assignments were based on imaging; precise bond order could not be determined from IM-STM alone.
results.quote:
Further exploring the limits of mechanosynthetic selectivity, under these z-only conditions 
with the silicon dimer center as the interaction point, donation occurred at a rate of 107/197 
interactions with EAOGe–C2I.

results.finding: A silicon dimer vacancy resulted from 2 successive abstractions at the same dimer site; sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The reported mechanosynthetic interactions were performed without applied bias. The result is a subtractive sequence on Si(100).
results.quote:
However, a second silicon abstraction event at the 
same dimer site yields a static silicon dimer vacancy (‘DV’, Fig. 4A), appearing as a dark 
depression, consistent with native dimer vacancy defects (26).

results.finding: Positioned molecular building blocks formed covalent dimers and trimers; sample size not reported.
results.detail: Coupling was induced by voltage pulses on bilayer NaCl/Cu(111) at 5.2 K; product connectivity was checked by imaging, manipulation and bond-length measurements.
results.quote:
Covalent 
homo-dimers in cis and trans configurations and homo-/hetero-trimers were selectively synthesized by a sequence of deha-
logenation, translational manipulation and intermolecular coupling of halogenated precursors.

results.finding: Sequential coupling extended a molecular dimer to a 3-block trimer; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The coupling reactions used voltage pulses, so the result does not meet the requirement for reactions driven by mechanical forces without an electric field.
results.quote:
Here a pyrene diradical is coupled 
with the dimer, generating a TPP 2• trimer (Fig. 4d).

results.finding: AI-assisted probe chemistry produced six-bond transformations in single-molecule quantum π-magnets; sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The transformation was voltage-controlled. The text does not establish fabrication of a complete structure from a blueprint without intervention for each reaction.
results.quote: A joint experimental and theoretical investigation demonstrates that a voltage-controlled two-electron-assisted electronic excitation enables synchronous six-bond transformations to extend the zigzag edge topology of single-molecule quantum π-magnets

results.finding: Hydrogen abstraction from a silicon probe succeeded in 27 of 28 trials.
results.detail: The authors report one mechanically controlled reaction per trial at zero bias. A second molecule imaged the same build site, but a second reaction there was proposed rather than demonstrated.
results.quote:
This outcome – removal of a single hydrogen atom at zero volts 
– was observed in 27 out of 28 trials, indicating that the process is well controlled and reproducible 
(Methods and Supplementary Section 10).
